source: Checked 2026-11-20 against hobby and restoration sources (forum and club pages, not factory documents): Model A bodies in pyroxylin lacquer, low gloss, beside high-gloss black enamel on fenders, splash aprons and running boards; engine bay in dull black japan; bright work nickel plated in 1928-29 (chrome over nickel on the radiator shell and bumpers from about 1930); closed-car roofs rubberized fabric over a wooden frame until the all-steel 'turret top' of 1935; many 1920s bodies steel panels on ash framing. Exact primer and baking steps for the Model A were not confirmed. Sources: mafca.com tech Q&A on paint, mtfca.com and fordbarn.com threads, modelaclub.com, finishing.com, Wikipedia 'Body solder' and 'Coachwork'.

body_lacquer.name: 차체 판 (래커)
body_lacquer.note: Steel panels, partly on ash framing; red-oxide primer, a grey surfacer sanded smooth, then thin coats of pyroxylin (nitrocellulose) lacquer: low gloss against the enamel fenders.

fender_enamel.name: 펜더 (구운 검은 에나멜)
fender_enamel.note: Black enamel, high gloss, on fenders, splash aprons and running boards; a baked prime coat under it (Model T practice; Model A steps unconfirmed).

running_board.name: 발판 (고무 매트)
running_board.note: Ribbed rubber mat on steel; scuffs rather than wears through.

roof_cloth.name: 지붕 가운데 (인조 가죽)
roof_cloth.note: Rubberized fabric over wooden bows and slats (closed cars until the 1935 all-steel turret top); torn, not scraped; replaced.

nickel.name: 니켈 도금 (황동 바탕)
nickel.note: 1928-29: nickel plate on brass or steel, buffs bright but dulls quickly; from about 1930 chrome over nickel on the radiator shell and bumpers.

engine_japan.name: 엔진룸 (무광 검은 재팬)
engine_japan.note: Dull black gasoline-resistant japan on engine-bay parts.

lead.alloy: lead-tin body solder, about 70/30 or 80/20 Pb/Sn
lead.flux: zinc chloride with ammonium chloride (tinning paste)
steps: clean to bright steel (scrape, file, steel wool)
tin: flux and a thin coat of solder wiped on
build up: solder stick softened with a torch, worked with an oak paddle greased with beeswax
lead.note: Lead was the filler at the factory and in shops until plastic fillers (about 1955).
